UX Research Artificial Intelligence Customer Experience User Experience Product Strategy Strategic UX Research UX Research in the Age of AI: When Everyone Can Build, Understanding People Becomes the Advantage Jasper Schon 8 min read · Nov 4, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Why understanding human needs, expectations and experiences is becoming a critical competitive advantage. Imagine a market where almost every company can build the same product. AI makes development faster, prototypes cheaper and experimentation easier. Features that once required months of work can now be built in a fraction of the time. Teams can test ideas, launch products and iterate at a pace that would have been difficult to imagine just a few years ago. That sounds like progress. And it is. But it also raises a more fundamental question: If everyone can build, what actually makes a product worth choosing? The answer is unlikely to be another feature. As AI changes the economics of building products, the ability to understand people becomes an increasingly important source of differentiation. This is where Strategic UX Research comes in. Not simply as a way to improve interfaces, but as a capability that helps organizations understand what people need, what they value and where meaningful opportunities exist. The product-building advantage is changing For a long time, the ability to build and deliver digital products was a competitive advantage in itself. Companies with the right technical capabilities, resources and development speed could create experiences that others struggled to replicate. AI is changing that equation. It lowers the barriers to prototyping, development and experimentation. More teams can explore ideas, build functional solutions and bring products to market. This creates enormous opportunities, but it also makes one thing harder: standing out. When building becomes easier, simply having the ability to build something is less of a differentiator. The question shifts from Can we build this? to Should we build this in the first place? That is not primarily a technical question. It requires an understanding of people, their context, their expectations and the problems they are actually trying to solve. More features don’t necessarily mean more value There is a tendency in product development to equate progress with output: more features, more functionality, more automation. But product value is not determined by the number of things a product can do. People don’t choose a product because it has the longest feature list. They choose it because it helps them achieve something, makes a task easier, gives them confidence or creates an experience they trust. And sometimes, what makes a product valuable is not what it offers, but how it makes people feel when using it. A financial product, for example, can offer competitive pricing and a technically sophisticated investment experience. But if customers struggle to get help when something goes wrong, the overall experience can quickly undermine the value of the product itself. This is not an abstract problem. It is something companies can observe in the market. When efficiency comes at the expense of experience Press enter or click to view image in full size Image: Trade Republic / Press Material Trade Republic offers an interesting example of what happens when functional differentiation becomes increasingly difficult. As a neobroker competing with providers like Scalable Capital and Trading 212, Trade Republic operates in a market where the core offering is becoming increasingly similar. Customers can access comparable investment products across these platforms, including stocks and ETFs, often at very similar price points. This reflects a broader shift towards what has often been described as the Experience Economy : as products and services become increasingly comparable, the experience surrounding them becomes a more important source of differentiation. Trade Republic built much of its proposition around accessibility, simplicity and automation. A streamlined app and digital-first customer service made it possible to serve a growing customer base efficiently. But efficiency and a good customer experience aren’t always the same thing. In 2025, the company faced growing public criticism over its customer support. Between January and September, German consumer advice centres recorded more than 300 complaints about Trade Republic, an increase of 133% compared with the same period in the previous year. The main criticism concerned difficulties reaching customer support and resolving issues. ( Tagesschau, November 10, 2025 ) For a financial platform, that’s particularly relevant. People might appreciate being able to invest with just a few taps. But when something goes wrong with their money, they don’t necessarily want another automated response. They want someone who understands their problem and can help resolve it. In April 2026, Trade Republic announced a major service initiative: 24/7 telephone and live-chat support with human agents.
